blocks.text: A barrel of crude pumped in the Niger Delta, a bag of cocoa in Ondo and a haircut in Kano are all part of what Nigeria produced this year. Adding them up without counting the same thing twice, and then asking how much of the income leaked abroad, is the work of national-income accounting — the scoreboard behind talk of growth, recession and per capita income.

blocks.title: GDP, GNP, NNP and per capita income
blocks.text: Gross Domestic Product is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders in a period. Gross National Product is GDP plus net income from abroad (income residents earn overseas minus income non-residents earn locally). Net National Product is GNP minus depreciation. Per capita income is national income (or GDP) divided by population.

blocks.markdown:
The links are mechanical and examiners test them as arithmetic:

- $\text{GNP} = \text{GDP} + \text{net factor income from abroad}$
- $\text{NNP} = \text{GNP} - \text{depreciation (capital consumption)}$
- $\text{NNP at factor cost}$ (national income) $= \text{NNP at market prices} - \text{indirect taxes} + \text{subsidies}$
- $\text{Per capita income} = \text{national income} \div \text{population}$

If Nigerians working in Ghana send home more than foreigners working in Nigeria send out, net income from abroad is positive and GNP exceeds GDP. Depreciation is the wearing-out of machines, vehicles and oil-field equipment; subtracting it stops us treating capital consumption as new output.

blocks.caption: In theory the three approaches give the same total; in practice statistical discrepancies appear

blocks.title: Computing GDP, GNP and NNP from given data
blocks.prompt: The following hypothetical figures, in billions of naira, are given for an economy: household consumption 400, investment 150, government spending 120, exports 80, imports 50, net factor income from abroad −20, depreciation 30. Calculate GDP, GNP and NNP.

steps.text: GDP by the expenditure approach is C + I + G + (X − M).
GNP = GDP + net income from abroad = 700 + (−20) = 680 billion naira. A negative NFIA means more factor income left the country than entered it.

blocks.answer: GDP ₦700 billion; GNP ₦680 billion; NNP ₦650 billion

items: **Double counting** — including both flour and the bread baked from it inflates GDP; use value added or final goods only.
**The informal and subsistence sector** — a large share of Nigerian output (street trade, own-food farming, unpaid housework) is poorly measured or omitted.
**Income distribution is hidden** — the same GDP per head can describe a fairly equal society or one in which oil rents accrue to a few.
**Non-market and illegal activity** — unpaid domestic work is left out; some illegal trades are missed.
**Quality, leisure and externalities** — a more reliable generator, shorter working hours, or oil-spill damage do not show up cleanly in the total.
**Transfer payments** must be excluded from the income approach, and **intermediate imports** handled carefully in expenditure.

blocks.markdown: Because of those problems, a rise in measured GDP does not automatically mean that the average Nigerian is better off. Per capita figures help with population growth, but they still say nothing about who received the extra income, how much capital was used up, or whether the output was food, schools or a gas flare.

blocks.title: Watch the sign of net income from abroad
blocks.text: GNP = GDP + NFIA. If NFIA is negative, GNP is smaller than GDP — common when foreign firms repatriate oil profits. Students who always add the figure, ignoring the minus sign, throw away an easy mark. Also: never add intermediate goods to final output.

points: GDP measures output produced inside the country; GNP adds net income from abroad; NNP subtracts depreciation; per capita income divides by population.
The output, income and expenditure approaches are three ways of counting the same flow.
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − depreciation.
Problems include double counting, the informal sector, hidden inequality, omitted non-market work and externalities.
A higher GDP is not by itself proof of improved welfare.
